narrative:
The model estimated a 12% chance that you will fail the final year. In practical terms, that is a low estimated risk: failure is not the expected outcome, and the model is far from certain. If remedial courses are required, they should be understood as a precautionary support measure rather than proof that failing is likely.

The model’s assessment was shaped most strongly by three factors, and all three pushed the estimate toward passing rather than failing. The strongest was your reason for choosing the school: selecting it for its reputation had the largest influence, lowering the estimated failure risk; among students who passed, choosing the school for the course itself was more common, while reputation was chosen by about 29%. The second strongest was your record of past class failures. You have none, matching the average among students who passed, and this also lowered the risk. The third was your intention to continue to higher education. You want to go on to higher education, as did all students in the comparison group who passed, and this again pointed toward passing.

To improve and secure your final year, keep attending consistently—your four absences are close to the passed-student average—use the family educational support you already have, and discuss with teachers how to structure study time, especially since two to five hours weekly is common but more may help. Treat remedial classes as targeted practice, not punishment.
